claim: CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats are fragile sequences that when expanded form DNA secondary structures and cause human disease.
source: CAG/CTG trinuncleotide repeats are fragile sequences that when expanded form DNA secondary structures and cause human disease.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about CAG/CTG repeats and their role in disease.

claim: CAG repeat stability depends on H2A copy 1 (H2A.1) but not copy 2 (H2A.2).
source: Although the two copies of H2A are nearly identical in amino acid sequence, CAG repeat stability depends on H2A copy 1 (H2A.1) but not copy 2 (H2A.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential effects of H2A.1 and H2A.2 deletions on CAG repeat stability.

claim: H2A.1 promotes high-fidelity homologous recombination, sister chromatid recombination (SCR), and break-induced replication whereas H2A.2 does not share these functions.
source: H2A.1 promotes high-fidelity homologous recombination, sister chromatid recombination (SCR), and break-induced replication whereas H2A.2 does not share these functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental assays presented in the manuscript including SCR assays and BIR assays.

claim: Both decreased SCR and the increase in CAG expansions were due to the unique Thr126 residue in H2A.1.
source: Both decreased SCR and the increase in CAG expansions were due to the unique Thr126 residue in H2A.1 and hta1Δ or hta1-T126A mutants were epistatic to deletion of the Polδ subunit Pol32, suggesting a role for H2A.1 in D-loop extension.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that T126A mutation phenocopies hta1Δ effects on SCR and CAG expansions.

claim: hta1Δ or hta1-T126A mutants were epistatic to deletion of the Polδ subunit Pol32, suggesting a role for H2A.1 in D-loop extension.
source: Both decreased SCR and the increase in CAG expansions were due to the unique Thr126 residue in H2A.1 and hta1Δ or hta1-T126A mutants were epistatic to deletion of the Polδ subunit Pol32, suggesting a role for H2A.1 in D-loop extension.
evidence: This claim is based on genetic epistasis analysis and inference about the mechanistic role of H2A.1.

claim: H2A.1 plays a greater repair-specific role compared to H2A.2 and may be a first step towards evolution of a repair-specific function for H2AX compared to H2A in mammalian cells.
source: We conclude that H2A.1 plays a greater repair-specific role compared to H2A.2 and may be a first step towards evolution of a repair-specific function for H2AX compared to H2A in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and evolutionary inference.

claim: The SQEL motif in the H2A C-terminal tail is phosphorylated at Ser129 (H2AX-Ser139 in mammals) by the Phosphoinositide 3-Kinase-Related Kinases (PIKKs), Mec1 and Tel1 (ATR and ATM in mammals) in response to DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) and stalled or collapsed replication forks.
source: In response to DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) and stalled or collapsed replication forks, the SQEL motif in the H2A C-terminal tail is phosphorylated at Ser129 (H2AX-Ser139 in mammals) by the Phosphoinositide 3-Kinase-Related Kinases (PIKKs), Mec1 and Tel1 (ATR and ATM in mammals) (Downs et al., 2000; Lisby et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: γH2A (γH2AX in mammals) marks the site of damage and is propagated along the chromatin, detectable up to 50 kb from the break site in yeast and megabases in mammalian cells.
source: This modification, termed γH2A (γH2AX in mammals), marks the site of damage and is propagated along the chromatin, detectable up to 50 kb from the break site in yeast (Shroff et al., 2004) and megabases in mammalian cells (Rogakou et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: γH2A/γH2AX occurs rapidly upon induction of a DSB, detectable within minutes after damage.
source: γH2A/γH2AX occurs rapidly upon induction of a DSB, detectable within minutes after damage (Shroff et al., 2004; Rogakou et al., 1999; Paull et al., 2000), and is required to initiate the cascade of histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and repair factor recruitment and retention necessary for repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: γH2A/γH2AX is required to initiate the cascade of histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and repair factor recruitment and retention necessary for repair.
source: γH2A/γH2AX occurs rapidly upon induction of a DSB, detectable within minutes after damage (Shroff et al., 2004; Rogakou et al., 1999; Paull et al., 2000), and is required to initiate the cascade of histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and repair factor recruitment and retention necessary for repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: H2A/H2AX K5ac, K15ub/ac, K36ac, K119ub, and Y142ph all contribute to DNA repair.
source: However, other modifiable residues in the H2A tails can also modulate repair factor binding: H2A/H2AX K5ac, K15ub/ac, K36ac, K119ub, and Y142ph all contribute to DNA repair (reviewed in Hunt et al., 2013; Jacquet et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In humans over a dozen H2A variants have been identified.
source: Whereas in humans over a dozen H2A variants have been identified (Albig et al., 1999; Bönisch and Hake, 2012), S. cerevisiae contains just three variants of H2A, encoded by HTA1, HTA2, and HTZ1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: S. cerevisiae contains just three variants of H2A, encoded by HTA1, HTA2, and HTZ1.
source: Whereas in humans over a dozen H2A variants have been identified (Albig et al., 1999; Bönisch and Hake, 2012), S. cerevisiae contains just three variants of H2A, encoded by HTA1, HTA2, and HTZ1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast histone variants.

claim: HTA1 and HTA2 encode canonical H2A and the two copies are nearly identical in amino acid sequence except for a direct alanine-threonine switch at positions 125/126 in the C-terminal tail.
source: HTA1 and HTA2 encode canonical H2A and the two copies are nearly identical in amino acid sequence except for a direct alanine-threonine switch at positions 125/126 in the C-terminal tail (Figure 1B); the underlying DNA sequence is 94% similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The underlying DNA sequence of HTA1 and HTA2 is 94% similar.
source: HTA1 and HTA2 encode canonical H2A and the two copies are nearly identical in amino acid sequence except for a direct alanine-threonine switch at positions 125/126 in the C-terminal tail (Figure 1B); the underlying DNA sequence is 94% similar.
evidence: This is a statement of sequence similarity based on sequence analysis.

claim: H2A-T126 is phosphorylatable in vivo, even in the absence of DNA damage.
source: H2A-T126 is phosphorylatable in vivo, even in the absence of DNA damage (Wyatt et al., 2003; Moore et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: H2A.Z has only 56% amino acid sequence homology to canonical H2A.
source: The third H2A variant, H2A.Z, has only 56% amino acid sequence homology to canonical H2A.
evidence: This is a statement of sequence homology based on sequence analysis.

claim: CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats can form abnormal secondary structures, such as hairpins and slip-stranded DNA.
source: CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats are in this category, as they can form abnormal secondary structures, such as hairpins and slip-stranded DNA (reviewed in McMurray, 1999; Usdin et al., 2015; Schmidt and Pearson, 2016), and break at a higher frequency than non-repetitive DNA (Freudenreich et al., 1998; Callahan et al., 2003; Nasar et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles and previous work.

claim: CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats break at a higher frequency than non-repetitive DNA.
source: CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats are in this category, as they can form abnormal secondary structures, such as hairpins and slip-stranded DNA (reviewed in McMurray, 1999; Usdin et al., 2015; Schmidt and Pearson, 2016), and break at a higher frequency than non-repetitive DNA (Freudenreich et al., 1998; Callahan et al., 2003; Nasar et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Once expanded (addition of repeat units), the repeat tract is increasingly unstable and prone to further expansion in a length-dependent manner.
source: Once expanded (addition of repeat units), the repeat tract is increasingly unstable and prone to further expansion in a length-dependent manner (reviewed in Usdin et al., 2015; Kim and Mirkin, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: CAG/CTG repeat expansion beyond a threshold length of approximately 35 repeats can lead to human disease, including Huntington's disease, myotonic muscular dystrophy, and several spinocerebellar ataxias.
source: CAG/CTG repeats are found throughout the human genome but repeat expansion beyond a threshold length of approximately 35 repeats can lead to human disease, including Huntington's disease, myotonic muscular dystrophy, and several spinocerebellar ataxias (Usdin et al., 2015; Mirkin, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge about trinucleotide repeat diseases.

claim: The CAG/CTG repeat is a strong nucleosome-positioning element, shown in vitro by nucleosome assembly assays and visualized by electron microscopy.
source: The CAG/CTG repeat is a strong nucleosome-positioning element, shown in vitro by nucleosome assembly assays and visualized by electron microscopy (Godde and Wolffe, 1996; Wang et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Secondary structures that occur at CAG/CTG repeats can interfere with DNA transactions, causing stalled or collapsed replication forks, gaps, nicks, and DSBs.
source: Secondary structures that occur at CAG/CTG repeats can interfere with DNA transactions, causing stalled or collapsed replication forks, gaps, nicks, and DSBs (Usdin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Histone H4 acetylation promotes high-fidelity HR during post-replication repair at CAG repeats.
source: We previously described a role for histone H4 acetylation in promoting high-fidelity HR during post-replication repair at CAG repeats (House et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Deletion of histone H2A.1 increased CAG repeat fragility and expansion frequency.
source: In a primary genetic screen for CAG repeat fragility and a secondary screen of CAG repeat instability, deletion of histone H2A.1 increased CAG repeat fragility and expansion frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of H2A.2 had no effect on repeat fragility or instability.
source: However, deletion of the second copy of this protein, H2A.2, had no effect on repeat fragility or instability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H2A.1 threonine 126 (T126) is required to prevent CAG expansions.
source: We found that H2A.1 threonine 126 (T126) is required to prevent CAG expansions and that expansions that arise in the absence of phosphorylatable T126 are dependent on Rad51, Rad52, Rad57, and the Polδ subunit, Pol32.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expansions that arise in the absence of phosphorylatable T126 are dependent on Rad51, Rad52, Rad57, and the Polδ subunit, Pol32.
source: We found that H2A.1 threonine 126 (T126) is required to prevent CAG expansions and that expansions that arise in the absence of phosphorylatable T126 are dependent on Rad51, Rad52, Rad57, and the Polδ subunit, Pol32.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing suppression of expansions in double mutants.

claim: H2A.1 and H2A.1-T126 are required for efficient SCR at non-repetitive DNA sequences.
source: In addition, we show that H2A.1 and H2A.1-T126 are required for efficient SCR at non-repetitive DNA sequences, and are working in the same pathway as the Polδ subunit Pol32.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SCR assays.

claim: H2A.1 and H2A.1-T126 are working in the same pathway as the Polδ subunit Pol32.
source: In addition, we show that H2A.1 and H2A.1-T126 are required for efficient SCR at non-repetitive DNA sequences, and are working in the same pathway as the Polδ subunit Pol32.
evidence: This claim is supported by epistasis analysis showing no additive effect in double mutants.

claim: H2A.1 is specifically important in mediating repair via BIR.
source: Finally, we show that H2A.1 is specifically important in mediating repair via BIR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BIR assays.

claim: Initial semi-quantitative and quantitative assays showed a 2-fold increase in the rate of 5-FOA-resistance (FOAR) in the hta1Δ mutant compared to the wild-type for a strain containing a YAC with a (CAG)85 repeat tract.
source: Initial semi-quantitative and quantitative assays showed a 2-fold increase in the rate of 5-FOA-resistance (FOAR) in the hta1Δ mutant compared to the wild-type for a strain containing a YAC with a (CAG)85 repeat tract, whereas the hta2Δ mutant did not deviate from wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fragility assays.

claim: The hta2Δ mutant did not deviate from wild-type in the rate of 5-FOA-resistance (FOAR).
source: Initial semi-quantitative and quantitative assays showed a 2-fold increase in the rate of 5-FOA-resistance (FOAR) in the hta1Δ mutant compared to the wild-type for a strain containing a YAC with a (CAG)85 repeat tract, whereas the hta2Δ mutant did not deviate from wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fragility assays.

claim: Upon further analysis using multiple independent hta1Δ transformants, a wide range of repeat fragility rates was observed and thus the increase over wild-type could not be statistically verified.
source: Upon further analysis using multiple independent hta1Δ transformants, we observed a wide range of repeat fragility rates and thus were unable to statistically verify the increase over wild-type (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The hta1Δ mutant is mildly sensitive to phleomycin and not sensitive to the other DNA damaging agents tested (MMS, CPT, HU).
source: The hta1Δ mutant is mildly sensitive to phleomycin and not sensitive to the other DNA damaging agents tested (MMS, CPT, HU) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is likely a mild defect in repair at the CAG repeat in the absence of H2A copy 1.
source: We conclude that there is likely a mild defect in repair at the CAG repeat in the absence of H2A copy 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fragility data and inference about repair defects.

claim: Expansion frequency is significantly increased in the hta1Δ mutant (7-fold increase over wild-type, p=2.7×10−5).
source: Deletion of the genes encoding the two copies of H2A differentially affect CAG repeat stability: expansion frequency is significantly increased in the hta1Δ mutant (7-fold increase over wild-type, p=2.7×10−5) while expansion frequency in the hta2Δ mutant is not significantly changed from wild-type (1.3-fold increase over wild-type, p=0.71) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: Expansion frequency in the hta2Δ mutant is not significantly changed from wild-type (1.3-fold increase over wild-type, p=0.71).
source: Deletion of the genes encoding the two copies of H2A differentially affect CAG repeat stability: expansion frequency is significantly increased in the hta1Δ mutant (7-fold increase over wild-type, p=2.7×10−5) while expansion frequency in the hta2Δ mutant is not significantly changed from wild-type (1.3-fold increase over wild-type, p=0.71) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: Contractions were increased 2.6-fold in the hta1Δ but not the hta2Δ mutant.
source: Contractions were increased 2.6-fold in the hta1Δ but not the hta2Δ mutant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: H2A.1 is required to suppress CAG instability while H2A.2 is not.
source: Thus, H2A.1 is required to suppress CAG instability while H2A.2 is not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of hta1Δ and hta2Δ on CAG stability.

claim: H2A.Z is deposited at a DSB during repair.
source: Since H2A.Z is deposited at a DSB during repair (Kalocsay et al., 2009), we tested whether it is required to maintain CAG repeat stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The htz1Δ mutant is sensitive to DNA damaging agents.
source: Although the htz1Δ mutant is sensitive to DNA damaging agents (Morillo-Huesca et al., 2010; Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011), deleting the HTZ1 gene did not affect repeat expansion frequency, though contractions were significantly increased in the htz1Δ mutant (2.1-fold over WT, p=3.1×10−6) (Figure 1E) (House et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deleting the HTZ1 gene did not affect repeat expansion frequency.
source: Although the htz1Δ mutant is sensitive to DNA damaging agents (Morillo-Huesca et al., 2010; Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011), deleting the HTZ1 gene did not affect repeat expansion frequency, though contractions were significantly increased in the htz1Δ mutant (2.1-fold over WT, p=3.1×10−6) (Figure 1E) (House et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Contractions were significantly increased in the htz1Δ mutant (2.1-fold over WT, p=3.1×10−6).
source: Although the htz1Δ mutant is sensitive to DNA damaging agents (Morillo-Huesca et al., 2010; Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011), deleting the HTZ1 gene did not affect repeat expansion frequency, though contractions were significantly increased in the htz1Δ mutant (2.1-fold over WT, p=3.1×10−6) (Figure 1E) (House et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: Deleting either HTB gene had no significant effect on repeat expansion frequency.
source: Deleting either HTB gene had no significant effect on repeat expansion frequency (Figure 1D), but contractions were somewhat elevated in the htb1Δ mutant (2-fold over WT, p=0.01)(Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Contractions were somewhat elevated in the htb1Δ mutant (2-fold over WT, p=0.01).
source: Deleting either HTB gene had no significant effect on repeat expansion frequency (Figure 1D), but contractions were somewhat elevated in the htb1Δ mutant (2-fold over WT, p=0.01)(Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: H2A.1, H2A.Z, and H2B.1 are required to prevent CAG contractions.
source: Therefore, H2A.1, H2A.Z, and H2B.1 are required to prevent CAG contractions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the contraction data for these mutants.

claim: Of the histone H2 proteins, only H2A.1 plays a significant role in preventing CAG repeat expansions.
source: However, of the histone H2 proteins, only H2A.1 plays a significant role in preventing CAG repeat expansions, suggesting some specialized role for H2A.1 that we have explored further.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expansion data for all H2 variants tested.

claim: Histone H2A is encoded by two nearly identical gene copies in S. cerevisiae, each paired with a copy of H2B and differentially regulated.
source: Histone H2A is encoded by two nearly identical gene copies in S. cerevisiae, each paired with a copy of H2B and differentially regulated (Norris and Osley, 1987) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: While transcription from the HTA1-HTB1 gene pair can be upregulated in the absence of HTA2, HTA2-HTB2 is transcribed at a constant rate.
source: While transcription from the HTA1-HTB1 gene pair can be upregulated in the absence of HTA2, HTA2-HTB2 is transcribed at a constant rate (Moran et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The H2A pools will be normal in an hta2Δ mutant, whereas an hta1Δ mutant may have a global decrease in H2A.
source: As a result, the H2A pools will be normal in an hta2Δ mutant, whereas an hta1Δ mutant may have a global decrease in H2A.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential regulation of HTA1 and HTA2.

claim: A second pathway of gene dosage compensation exists in which the HTA2-HTB2 gene pair amplifies to form a minichromosome (that also contains the HHT1-HHF1 (H3-H4) gene pair) in the absence of HTA1-HTB1.
source: A second pathway of gene dosage compensation exists in which the HTA2-HTB2 gene pair amplifies to form a minichromosome (that also contains the HHT1-HHF1 (H3-H4) gene pair) in the absence of HTA1-HTB1 (35).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (reference 35).

claim: Equal expression of H2A proteins was confirmed by Western blot in the hta1Δ::HTA2 strain.
source: Equal expression of H2A proteins was confirmed by Western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No instances of gene amplification were detected at the genomic level by qPCR in strains tested for gene amplification of HTA1 or HTA2.
source: We tested strains for gene amplification of HTA1 or HTA2 by qPCR and no instances of gene amplification were detected at the genomic level (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR analysis.

claim: CAG repeat expansions remained significantly increased from the wild-type in the hta1Δ::HTA2 strain (p=4.2×10−4 to WT).
source: However, we observed that CAG repeat expansions remained significantly increased from the wild-type in the hta1Δ::HTA2 strain (p=4.2×10−4 to WT, Figure 1D), though a partial suppression of contractions was observed (Figure 1E)(Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: A partial suppression of contractions was observed in the hta1Δ::HTA2 strain.
source: However, we observed that CAG repeat expansions remained significantly increased from the wild-type in the hta1Δ::HTA2 strain (p=4.2×10−4 to WT, Figure 1D), though a partial suppression of contractions was observed (Figure 1E)(Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: While CAG contractions appear to be sensitive to overall histone levels, H2A.2 cannot compensate for H2A.1 in preventing repeat expansions, even when expressed at H2A.1 levels under control of the HTA1 promoter.
source: Therefore, while CAG contractions appear to be sensitive to overall histone levels, H2A.2 cannot compensate for H2A.1 in preventing repeat expansions, even when expressed at H2A.1 levels under control of the HTA1 promoter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hta1Δ::HTA2 experimental data.

claim: The sequence of H2A.1, not histone levels or subtleties in expression timing, is required to prevent CAG repeat expansions.
source: We conclude that the sequence of H2A.1, not histone levels or subtleties in expression timing, is required to prevent CAG repeat expansions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hta1Δ::HTA2 experimental data.

claim: Overall bulk chromatin structure was not altered in an hta1∆htb1∆ strain, though some areas of the genome were more sensitive to micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion.
source: Although overall bulk chromatin structure was not altered in an hta1∆htb1∆ strain, some areas of the genome were more sensitive to micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion (Norris et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A series of discrete, protected fragments (~5 nucleosomes), is observed at the CAG repeat, indicating several positioned nucleosomes within and flanking the CAG repeat.
source: A series of discrete, protected fragments (~5 nucleosomes), is observed, indicating several positioned nucleosomes within and flanking the CAG repeat (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A from MNase digestion and indirect end-labeling.

claim: The pattern is consistent with canonical ~165 bp spacing between nucleosomes, and suggests there is no visible, major disruption to the chromatin structure in the hta1∆ cells compared to the wild-type.
source: The pattern is consistent with canonical ~165 bp spacing between nucleosomes, and suggests there is no visible, major disruption to the chromatin structure in the hta1∆ cells compared to the wild-type (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MNase digestion data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The CAG repeat-containing probes produced a peak in intensity compared to the flanking, non-CAG repeat-containing probes, indicating strong nucleosomal protection at the CAG repeat.
source: The CAG repeat-containing probes produced a peak in intensity compared to the flanking, non-CAG repeat-containing probes, indicating strong nucleosomal protection at the CAG repeat (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B from Illumina array analysis.

claim: The CAG repeat positions a nucleosome in vivo on a yeast chromosome.
source: This result confirms previous in vitro data that the CAG repeat is a strong nucleosome binding sequence (Wang et al., 1994; Wang and Griffith, 1995; Volle and Delaney, 2012) and that it positions a nucleosome in vivo on a yeast chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Illumina array data and citations to previous in vitro work.

claim: The protection was not reduced in the hta1Δ and hta2Δ mutants.
source: The protection was not reduced in the hta1Δ and hta2Δ mutants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nucleosome positioning is not the major contributing factor to CAG instability in the hta1Δ mutant.
source: Thus, both methods used show that there is a positioned nucleosome at the CAG tract that is not altered in the hta1Δ background. We conclude that nucleosome positioning is not the major contributing factor to CAG instability in the hta1Δ mutant; however, subtle differences in chromatin structure in the absence of H2A.1 that are not visible by these assays may still impact repair pathway selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the nucleosome positioning data.

claim: Subtle differences in chromatin structure in the absence of H2A.1 that are not visible by these assays may still impact repair pathway selection.
source: Thus, both methods used show that there is a positioned nucleosome at the CAG tract that is not altered in the hta1Δ background. We conclude that nucleosome positioning is not the major contributing factor to CAG instability in the hta1Δ mutant; however, subtle differences in chromatin structure in the absence of H2A.1 that are not visible by these assays may still impact repair pathway selection.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible effects not detected by the assays.

claim: Previous work measuring steady state levels of 32P-labeled histones showed H2A phosphorylation was decreased ~2 fold in an hta1-T126A mutant, identifying T126 as a phosphorylatable residue.
source: Previous work measuring steady state levels of 32P-labeled histones showed H2A phosphorylation was decreased ~2 fold in an hta1-T126A mutant, identifying T126 as a phosphorylatable residue (Wyatt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When T126 was rendered non-modifiable by mutation to alanine, expansions were significantly increased over wild-type (3.7-fold over WT, p=0.04 to WT).
source: When T126 was rendered non-modifiable by mutation to alanine, expansions were significantly increased over wild-type (3.7-fold over WT, p=0.04 to WT) (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Deletion of HTA2 (hta1-T126A hta2Δ) had no further impact on CAG expansion frequency.
source: Deletion of HTA2 (hta1-T126A hta2Δ) had no further impact on CAG expansion frequency (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Expression of hta1-T126A from a plasmid in an hta1Δhta2Δ background resulted in a similar increase in expansions (3.1-fold over WT; p=0.04 to WT).
source: Expression of hta1-T126A from a plasmid in an hta1Δhta2Δ background resulted in a similar increase in expansions (3.1-fold over WT; p=0.04 to WT)(Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: The H2A.1-T126 residue is required for efficient repair of the CAG repeat to prevent expansions.
source: Therefore, the H2A.1-T126 residue is required for efficient repair of the CAG repeat to prevent expansions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the T126A mutation data.

claim: Phosphorylation of T126 would be lost in the T126A mutant, suggesting the possibility that phosphorylation of this residue is important for its role in repair.
source: Since phosphorylation of T126 would be lost in the T126A mutant, this suggests the possibility that phosphorylation of this residue is important for its role in repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the T126A mutation data.

claim: CAG expansion frequency remained elevated in the T126E mutant (4.9%, 3.7-fold over WT, p=0.01).
source: CAG expansion frequency remained elevated in the T126E mutant (4.9%, 3.7-fold over WT, p=0.01) (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Either dynamic phosphorylation of H2A.1-T126 or another characteristic of having a threonine at position 126 is important for promoting CAG stability.
source: This result suggests that either dynamic phosphorylation of H2A.1-T126 or another characteristic of having a threonine at position 126 is important for promoting CAG stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the T126E mutation data showing that constitutive phospho-mimic does not rescue the phenotype.

claim: The position of the threonine within the tail affects the efficiency with which the H2A copies contribute to DNA replication or repair.
source: Given the specific role for H2A.1, this result suggests that the position of the threonine within the tail affects the efficiency with which the H2A copies contribute to DNA replication or repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential roles of H2A.1 and H2A.2 and the T126 mutation data.

claim: CAG contractions were relatively unaffected in both the hta1-T126A and hta1-T126E mutants.
source: CAG contractions were relatively unaffected in both the hta1-T126A and hta1-T126E mutants (Supplementary file 2), therefore this residue primarily protects against expansions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The T126 residue primarily protects against expansions.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the suppression data in multiple double mutants.

claim: The CAG expansions observed in the absence of H2A.1 occur during a Pol32-dependent recombination process.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the CAG expansions observed in the absence of H2A.1 occur during a Pol32-dependent recombination process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined genetic data.

claim: H2A.1 could promote efficient D-loop extension during replication of the donor strand, thereby preventing opportunity for DNA secondary structure formation.
source: For example, H2A.1 could promote efficient D-loop extension during replication of the donor strand, thereby preventing opportunity for DNA secondary structure formation.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how H2A.1 prevents CAG expansions.

claim: Pol32 is known to be especially important for BIR, which involves extended D-loop synthesis that can proceed for many kilobases.
source: Pol32 is known to be especially important for BIR, which involves extended D-loop synthesis that can proceed for many kilobases (Lydeard et al., 2007; Anand et al., 2013; Malkova and Ira, 2013) (see also Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BIR frequency is suppressed 2.3-fold from wild-type in the hta1Δ mutant (p=1.0×10−4 to WT).
source: BIR frequency is suppressed 2.3-fold from wild-type in the hta1Δ mutant (p=1.0×10−4 to WT), but remains at wild-type levels in the hta2Δ mutant (Figure 5D) and the hta1-T126A mutant (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claim: BIR frequency remains at wild-type levels in the hta2Δ mutant and the hta1-T126A mutant.
source: BIR frequency is suppressed 2.3-fold from wild-type in the hta1Δ mutant (p=1.0×10−4 to WT), but remains at wild-type levels in the hta2Δ mutant (Figure 5D) and the hta1-T126A mutant (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Supplementary file 6.

claim: While H2A.1 is important for BIR, this function is either not regulated by T126 or the T126A phenotype was too subtle to be revealed by this assay.
source: Therefore, while H2A.1 is important for BIR, this function is either not regulated by T126 or the T126A phenotype was too subtle to be revealed by this assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BIR data showing hta1Δ but not hta1-T126A has a defect.

claim: Histone loss in response to DSBs has been implicated in promoting recombination and DNA repair rates.
source: Interestingly, histone loss in response to DSBs has been implicated in promoting recombination and DNA repair rates (Hauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Given that the BIR system depends on an induced DSB, altered histone levels in the hta1Δ mutant may increase gene conversions or other conservative repair pathways at the expense of BIR.
source: Therefore, given that the BIR system depends on an induced DSB, altered histone levels in the hta1Δ mutant may increase gene conversions or other conservative repair pathways at the expense of BIR.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the BIR defect in hta1Δ based on previous work about histone loss.

claim: The repair outcome profile in the hta1Δ mutant is altered from wild-type as a greater proportion of cells undergo other types of repair instead of BIR.
source: The repair outcome profile in the hta1Δ mutant is altered from wild-type as a greater proportion of cells undergo other types of repair instead of BIR (Figure 5E) (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The increase in other types of repair events in the hta1Δ mutant is similar to the phenotype in the pol32Δ mutant, and therefore is likely a consequence of decreased BIR rates.
source: While less severe, the increase in these other types of repair events in the hta1Δ mutant is similar to the phenotype in the pol32Δ mutant, and therefore is likely a consequence of decreased BIR rates (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of repair outcome profiles.

claim: Deletion of H2A.1 results in decreased BIR and alterations in repair type frequencies, demonstrating that H2A.1 plays a role in facilitating efficient BIR.
source: We conclude that deletion of H2A.1 results in decreased BIR and alterations in repair type frequencies, demonstrating that H2A.1 plays a role in facilitating efficient BIR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BIR assay data.

claim: Expansions in the hta1Δ mutant may be due to defective D-loop extension, since this step occurs during both SCR and BIR.
source: Together with the SCR data, this suggests that expansions in the hta1Δ mutant may be due to defective D-loop extension, since this step occurs during both SCR and BIR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined SCR and BIR data.

claim: The absence of gene product from HTA1 and HTB1 led to a constitutive heat shock response after exposure to high temperature, and this phenotype was not rescued with an additional copy of HTA2 and HTB2.
source: The histone subtypes have been documented before to play different functions during the S. cerevisiae life cycle. The absence of gene product from HTA1 and HTB1 led to a constitutive heat shock response after exposure to high temperature, and this phenotype was not rescued with an additional copy of HTA2 and HTB2 (33).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (reference 33).

claim: H2A.1 is specifically important for repair or recovery from DNA damage.
source: Taken with our results demonstrating differential roles for the H2A copies in preventing HR-mediated CAG repeat expansions, facilitating sister chromatid recombination, and promoting BIR, this further supports that H2A.1 is specifically important for repair or recovery from DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from this study and previous work.

claim: H2A.1 is more efficient at promoting high-fidelity HR than H2A.2 because of protein sequence; specifically, the position of the phosphorylatable threonine in the H2A.1 C-terminal tail is more advantageous to repair than H2A.2.
source: Our data indicate that H2A.1 is more efficient at promoting high-fidelity HR than H2A.2 because of protein sequence; specifically, the position of the phosphorylatable threonine in the H2A.1 C-terminal tail is more advantageous to repair than H2A.2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential roles of H2A.1 and H2A.2 and the T126 data.

claim: Both copies of yeast H2A contain the SQEL motif in the C-terminal tail, and therefore both copies are considered homologs of mammalian H2AX.
source: Both copies of yeast H2A contain the SQEL motif in the C-terminal tail, and therefore both copies are considered homologs of mammalian H2AX.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast H2A and mammalian H2AX.

claim: Yeast H2A.1 is in fact the closer homolog of mammalian H2AX, as it plays a greater HR-specific role than H2A.2.
source: A compelling implication of our result here is that yeast H2A.1 is in fact the closer homolog of mammalian H2AX, as it plays a greater HR-specific role than H2A.2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data showing H2A.1 has a greater repair role.

claim: Like H2A.1, mammalian H2AX also contains a phosphorylatable threonine two residues before serine 139.
source: Like H2A.1, mammalian H2AX also contains a phophorylatable threonine two residues before serine 139.
evidence: This is a statement of sequence similarity based on sequence alignment.

claim: Similar to H2AX, H2A.1 is initially a smaller proportion of the total H2A pool.
source: Also similar to H2AX, H2A.1 is initially a smaller proportion of the total H2A pool (Moran et al., 1990; Rogakou et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeast H2A.1 and H2A.2 may be more akin to histone variants than histone copies.
source: Consequently, yeast H2A.1 and H2A.2 may be more akin to histone variants than histone copies.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the functional differences between H2A.1 and H2A.2.

claim: H2A-Thr126 has previously been shown to be phosphorylated in vivo but its phosphorylation state after DNA damage and its overall contribution to break repair was unclear.
source: H2A-Thr126 has previously been shown to be phosphorylated in vivo but its phosphorylation state after DNA damage and its overall contribution to break repair was unclear (Wyatt et al., 2003; Moore et al., 2007; Harvey et al., 2005; Chambers and Downs, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: H2A.1-T126 is important for maintaining CAG repeats and plays a role in promoting efficient SCR.
source: Using a naturally unstable expanded CAG repeat tract, we have shown that H2A.1-T126 is important for maintaining CAG repeats and plays a role in promoting efficient SCR.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the CAG stability and SCR assays.

claim: Overall levels of HR/SCR are suppressed in the absence of H2A.1-T126, and the recombination that does take place proceeds with low fidelity, leading to repeat expansions.
source: Our results indicate that overall levels of HR/SCR are suppressed in the absence of H2A.1-T126, and that the recombination that does take place proceeds with low fidelity, leading to repeat expansions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined SCR and CAG expansion data.

claim: It is formally possible that some other physical property of threonine at position 126 may be important for repair, rather than phosphorylation per se.
source: Although our results implicate a requirement for phosphorylation of H2A.1-T126 in DNA repair, it is formally possible that some other physical property of threonine at position 126 may be important for repair, rather than phosphosphorylation per se.
evidence: This is a caveat to the interpretation that phosphorylation is required.

claim: The amino acid sequence in the H2A.1 C-terminal tail with threonine at position 126 may be more advantageous to DNA repair factor recruitment, independent of T126 modification status.
source: For example, the amino acid sequence in the H2A.1 C-terminal tail with threonine at position 126 may be more advantageous to DNA repair factor recruitment, independent of T126 modification status.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the importance of T126.

claim: H2A.1-T126 could influence neighboring modifications, such as S122 phosphorylation or acetylation of K124 or K127.
source: Alternatively, H2A.1-T126 could influence neighboring modifications, such as S122 phosphorylation or acetylation of K124 or K127, though our data indicate that T126 does not modulate S129 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility for how T126 could affect repair.

claim: The fact that expansions, an addition of bases, occur in hta1Δ and hta1-T126A mutants is most supportive of a role for H2A.1 in promoting a synthesis step of DNA repair.
source: The fact that expansions, an addition of bases, occur in hta1Δ and hta1-T126A mutants is most supportive of a role for H2A.1 in promoting a synthesis step of DNA repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the expansions observed.

claim: The expansions are likely arising downstream of synapsis and D-loop assembly since they were suppressed in the absence of Rad51, Rad52, and Rad57.
source: The expansions are likely arising downstream of synapsis and D-loop assembly since they were suppressed in the absence of Rad51, Rad52, and Rad57 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the suppression data in HR mutants.

claim: H2A.1 and T126 play no role in repair via SSA, which does not require formation of a D-loop.
source: Similarly, H2A.1 and T126 play no role in repair via SSA, which does not require formation of a D-loop (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the SSA assay.

claim: H2A.1 is most likely promoting efficient D-loop extension during replication of the donor strand.
source: Further, our data placing H2A.1 and T126 in the same pathway as Pol32 in the unequal SCR assay supports a role during D-loop extension. Therefore, we conclude that H2A.1 is most likely promoting efficient D-loop extension during replication of the donor strand.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined genetic and epistasis data.

claim: H2A.1-T126 could be required to promote a later step in the process such as D-loop resolution or re-establishment of the chromatin structure of the repaired gap, which could explain why the H2A.1-T126A mutant did not have a discernable effect on BIR.
source: A second possibility is that H2A.1-T126 is required to promote a later step in the process such as D-loop resolution or re-establishment of the chromatin structure of the repaired gap. This could explain why the H2A.1-T126A mutant did not have a discernable effect on BIR, which does not include re-engagement of the extended D-loop with the initiating DNA molecule.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the role of H2A.1-T126.

claim: The role of H2A.1-T126 was not directly dependent on S129ph, however, the two residues could act together to affect an outcome.
source: Our data indicated that the role of H2A.1-T126 was not directly dependent on S129ph, however, the two residues could act together to affect an outcome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic data and speculation about possible interactions.

claim: H2A-S129ph begins to accumulate at the CAG repeat 20 min into S-phase and peaks at 40 min.
source: H2A-S129ph begins to accumulate at the CAG repeat 20 min into S-phase and peaks at 40 min (House et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: H2A.1 is either incorporated or phosphorylated at the CAG tract 40 min into S-phase, appearing only after initial accumulation of S129ph but coinciding with peak S129ph.
source: H2A.1 is either incorporated or phosphorylated at the CAG tract 40 min into S-phase, appearing only after initial accumulation of S129ph but coinciding with peak S129ph.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP timing data.

claim: Specific incorporation of H2A.1 at the CAG repeat when DNA damage is occurring is highly suggestive of some role for T126 at that time.
source: Specific incorporation of H2A.1 at the CAG repeat when DNA damage is occurring is highly suggestive of some role for T126 at that time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of H2A.1 enrichment.

claim: The additional ChIP signal could be due to existing H2A.1 becoming phosphorylated locally.
source: Since our antibody also detects phosphorylated H2A.1, it could be that the additional ChIP signal is due to existing H2A.1 becoming phosphorylated locally.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the ChIP signal.

claim: The ChIP signal may reflect damage-specific incorporation of H2A.1, which may or may not be phosphorylated on T126.
source: Alternatively it may reflect damage-specific incorporation of H2A.1, which may or may not be phosphorylated on T126 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the ChIP signal.

claim: Whole-genome proteomics did not identify H2A-T126ph as a DNA damage-inducible modification.
source: Levels of H2A.1-T126 decreased upon MMS damage (Figure 3E), and whole-genome proteomics did not identify H2A-T126ph as a DNA damage-inducible modification (Bastos de Oliveira et al., 2015; Smolka et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2016), though because T126 is surrounded by two lysines (K124, K127), it will end up on a peptide only three amino acids long after trypsin digest, which will not be easily detected by mass spectrometry.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous proteomics studies, with a caveat about detection limitations.

claim: T126ph is a pre-existing modification independent of S129ph, but these two modifications may work together to promote efficient repair, for example by binding or excluding certain repair factors in a combinatorial fashion.
source: Nonetheless, we favor a model in which T126ph is a pre-existing modification independent of S129ph, but that these two modifications may work together to promote efficient repair, for example by binding or excluding certain repair factors in a combinatorial fashion.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how T126ph and S129ph might function.

claim: In this scenario, T126ph would become enriched at the site of damage because of damage-specific incorporation of H2A.1 during repair and disappear after repair is complete, either by removal of H2A.1 or local dephosphorylation of the T126 residue.
source: In this scenario, T126ph would become enriched at the site of damage because of damage-specific incorporation of H2A.1 during repair (Figure 6) and disappear after repair is complete, either by removal of H2A.1 or local dephosphorylation of the T126 residue.
evidence: This is a speculative model for the dynamics of T126ph during repair.

claim: Depending on the phosphorylation status of both residues, a repair protein could recognize one or both residues, which could facilitate removal of S129ph-bound proteins or turnover of S129ph/T126ph-containing nucleosomes, influencing the overall progression of the repair process.
source: Depending on the phosphorylation status of both residues, a repair protein could recognize one or both residues, which could facilitate removal of S129ph-bound proteins or turnover of S129ph/T126ph-containing nucleosomes, influencing the overall progression of the repair process.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how combinatorial modifications could affect repair.

claim: The similar increase in expansions in the T126A and T126E mutants suggests that dephosphorylation of T126 could be important for repair fidelity.
source: This idea is supported by the similar increase in expansions in the T126A and T126E mutants, suggesting that dephosphorylation of T126 could be important for repair fidelity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the T126A and T126E mutation data.

claim: The presence of a threonine three amino acids away from S129ph, independently of its modification state, could influence repair.
source: Alternatively, the presence of a threonine three amino acids away from S129ph, independently of its modification state, could influence repair, or the T126 effect may be independent of S129ph, even though they occur coincidentally.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the role of T126.

claim: The T126 effect may be independent of S129ph, even though they occur coincidentally.
source: Alternatively, the presence of a threonine three amino acids away from S129ph, independently of its modification state, could influence repair, or the T126 effect may be independent of S129ph, even though they occur coincidentally.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the relationship between T126 and S129ph.

claim: In G2/M when a sister chromatid is available for recombination, γH2A is dispensible for recruitment of several chromatin modifiers, including Ino80 and subunits of RSC, NuA4, Rpd3, SWI/SNF, and SWR-C.
source: Interestingly, in G2/M when a sister chromatid is available for recombination, γH2A is dispensible for recruitment of several chromatin modifiers, including Ino80 and subunits of RSC, NuA4, Rpd3, SWI/SNF, and SWR-C (Bennett et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: H2A.1-T126-mediated recruitment of chromatin remodelers could be important for opening the chromatin structure to allow access by repair factors, remodeling chromatin on the donor strand to facilitate synapsis or D-loop extension, or resetting the chromatin to promote repair resolution.
source: H2A.1-T126-mediated recruitment of chromatin remodelers could be important for opening the chromatin structure to allow access by repair factors, remodeling chromatin on the donor strand to facilitate synapsis or D-loop extension, or resetting the chromatin to promote repair resolution.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how H2A.1-T126 could function through chromatin remodelers.

claim: The hta1-T126A mutant displays a defect in telomere positioning effect (TPE).
source: The hta1-T126A mutant displays a defect in telomere positioning effect (TPE) (Wyatt et al., 2003), consistent with a role in reestablishing chromatin structure after repair or replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RSC and NuA4 are required to promote high-fidelity repair of the CAG repeat.
source: We previously found that RSC and NuA4 are required to promote high-fidelity repair of the CAG repeat, and showed that RSC subunits are recruited to the repeat during S-phase (RSC2 peaks at 20 min, RSC1 at 40 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: RSC subunits are recruited to the repeat during S-phase (RSC2 peaks at 20 min, RSC1 at 40 min).
source: We previously found that RSC and NuA4 are required to promote high-fidelity repair of the CAG repeat, and showed that RSC subunits are recruited to the repeat during S-phase (RSC2 peaks at 20 min, RSC1 at 40 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: RSC and NuA4 are promoting post-replication repair events.
source: We concluded that these factors are promoting post-replication repair events (House et al., 2014b), however, it is possible that RSC and NuA4 also have a more general role in any D-loop mediated repair process.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous work with a caveat about possible broader roles.

claim: Recruitment of chromatin remodelers to the CAG repeat during repair could facilitate chromatin remodeling to promote efficient D-loop progression or resolution and high-fidelity repair.
source: Recruitment of any of these proteins to the CAG repeat during repair could facilitate chromatin remodeling to promote efficient D-loop progression or resolution and high-fidelity repair.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how chromatin remodelers could function at the CAG repeat.

claim: Hairpins formed by CAG or CTG repeats interfere with replication and induce joint molecules between sister chromatids, which have been visualized by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis.
source: Hairpins formed by CAG or CTG repeats interfere with replication and induce joint molecules between sister chromatids, which have been visualized by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis (Kerrest et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gaps caused by replication bypass of the CAG repeat are repaired via SCR, and incorporation of H2A.1 and/or H2A.1-T126ph ensures efficient remodeling and progression of Pol32-mediated D-loop extension, leading to high-fidelity repair.
source: We propose a model in which gaps caused by replication bypass of the CAG repeat are repaired via SCR, and that incorporation of H2A.1 and/or H2A.1-T126ph ensures efficient remodeling and progression of Pol32-mediated D-loop extension, leading to high-fidelity repair (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined data from the study.

claim: In the absence of H2A.1, suboptimal signaling from the H2A.2-T125 residue may inefficiently recruit or retain chromatin remodelers or other DNA repair proteins, impeding D-loop extension due to a chromatin state that is not permissive to extension and copying.
source: In the absence of H2A.1, suboptimal signaling from the H2A.2-T125 residue may inefficiently recruit or retain chromatin remodelers or other DNA repair proteins, impeding D-loop extension due to a chromatin state that is not permissive to extension and copying (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposed model for the defect in the absence of H2A.1.

claim: Inefficient progression of the recombination intermediate could lead to Polδ stalling or transient dissociation of the 3' end of the invading strand, which would allow opportunity for CAG repeat secondary structure formation and slippage during synthesis, leading to repeat length changes in the repaired DNA strand.
source: Inefficient progression of the recombination intermediate could lead to Polδ stalling or transient dissociation of the 3' end of the invading strand, which would allow opportunity for CAG repeat secondary structure formation and slippage during synthesis, leading to repeat length changes in the repaired DNA strand.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for how expansions arise.

claim: Chromatin remodelers or repair factors influenced by the presence of H2A.1-T126 may be required to reset the chromatin structure after repair, and the permissive chromatin state could allow multiple, aberrant invasion events that would increase the opportunity for misalignments during D-loop initiation or elongation, resulting in repeat instability.
source: Alternatively, chromatin remodelers or repair factors influenced by the presence of H2A.1-T126 may be required to reset the chromatin structure after repair. The permissive chromatin state could allow multiple, aberrant invasion events that would increase the opportunity for misalignments during D-loop initiation or elongation, resulting in repeat instability.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanistic explanation for repeat instability.

claim: A replication fork stalled by a CAG or CTG hairpin may be converted to a one-ended DSB that could facilitate HR-dependent fork restart, similar to BIR (e.g. broken fork repair or BFR).
source: Perhaps less commonly, a replication fork stalled by a CAG or CTG hairpin may be converted to a one-ended DSB that could facilitate HR-dependent fork restart, similar to BIR (e.g. broken fork repair or BFR; Malkova and Ira, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative model for an alternative pathway that could lead to expansions.

claim: If fork restart proceeds with low fidelity, such as if recombination structures are misaligned or hairpins cause strand slippage, mutations can arise.
source: If fork restart proceeds with low fidelity, such as if recombination structures are misaligned or hairpins cause strand slippage, mutations can arise.
evidence: This is a general statement about how low-fidelity repair can lead to mutations.

claim: Recovery from broken forks via BIR/BFR has recently been proposed to cause large-scale expansions of a (CAG)140 repeat tract in yeast.
source: Indeed, recovery from broken forks via BIR/BFR has recently been proposed to cause large-scale expansions of a (CAG)140 repeat tract in yeast (Kim et al., 2017), and our data at the (CAG)85 repeat are consistent with these results.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The data at the (CAG)85 repeat are consistent with BIR/BFR causing large-scale expansions.
source: Indeed, recovery from broken forks via BIR/BFR has recently been proposed to cause large-scale expansions of a (CAG)140 repeat tract in yeast (Kim et al., 2017), and our data at the (CAG)85 repeat are consistent with these results.
evidence: This is a statement of consistency between the current data and previous work.

claim: In the wild-type background, expansion frequency is significantly increased in a pol32Δ mutant where BIR is suppressed, indicating that BIR is not the only pathway creating expansions.
source: However, in the wild-type background, expansion frequency is significantly increased in a pol32Δ mutant where BIR is suppressed (Figure 5B), indicating that BIR is not the only pathway creating expansions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pol32Δ expansion data.

claim: At least some expansions in the pol32Δ mutant occur during recombination.
source: Our data show that at least some expansions in the pol32Δ mutant occur during recombination (Figure 5B), suggesting that efficient D-loop synthesis through a CAG repeat requires Pol32.
evidence: This claim is supported by the suppression of expansions in pol32Δrad51Δ double mutant.

claim: Efficient D-loop synthesis through a CAG repeat requires Pol32.
source: Our data show that at least some expansions in the pol32Δ mutant occur during recombination (Figure 5B), suggesting that efficient D-loop synthesis through a CAG repeat requires Pol32.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pol32Δ expansion data.

claim: Some expansions occurring in the pol32Δ mutant may be arising by a different mechanism, such as impaired Polδ synthesis during replication.
source: It remains possible that some expansions occurring in the pol32Δ mutant are arising by a different mechanism, such as impaired Polδ synthesis during replication.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for some expansions in pol32Δ.

claim: While efficient BIR was dependent on H2A.1, the rates were not affected in the hta1-T126A mutant, thus, the requirement of H2A.1 during BIR is not through the modifiable T126.
source: While efficient BIR was dependent on H2A.1, the rates were not affected in the hta1-T126A mutant, thus, the requirement of H2A.1 during BIR is not through the modifiable T126.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential BIR phenotypes of hta1Δ and hta1-T126A.

claim: The BIR assay involves a DSB whereas the spontaneous SCR assay and CAG repeat expansion assay is measuring the response at endogenous DNA lesions that will include a mix of nicks, gaps, and a small proportion of DSBs.
source: The BIR assay involves a DSB whereas the spontaneous SCR assay and CAG repeat expansion assay is measuring the response at endogenous DNA lesions that will include a mix of nicks, gaps, and a small proportion of DSBs.
evidence: This is a statement about the differences between the assay systems.

claim: CAG fragility, CAG contractions, and BIR, that all involve an initiating DSB, were dependent on H2A.1 but not the T126 residue.
source: We note that CAG fragility, CAG contractions, and BIR, that all involve an initiating DSB, were dependent on H2A.1 but not the T126 residue.
evidence: This is a summary of the differential requirements for H2A.1 vs T126 across different assays.

claim: The data are consistent with H2A.1 levels affecting DSB repair while the H2A.1 sequence-specific role is during gap repair/SCR.
source: Therefore, our data are consistent with H2A.1 levels affecting DSB repair while the H2A.1 sequence-specific role is during gap repair/SCR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential phenotypes across assay types.

claim: Recombination can itself be mutagenic if it does not proceed in a regulated manner.
source: At the occurrence of DNA damage, recombination is thought to be more protective to genome integrity than end joining because the repair is templated. However, recombination can itself be mutagenic if it does not proceed in a regulated manner (Polleys et al., 2017; Guirouilh-Barbat et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Turnover of chromatin modifications during repair is an attractive model for facilitating proper repair progression, either by influencing chromatin reorganization or by facilitating sequential recruitment and release of repair factors.
source: Turnover of chromatin modifications during repair is an attractive model for facilitating proper repair progression, either by influencing chromatin reorganization (reviewed in Polo, 2015) or by facilitating sequential recruitment and release of repair factors (reviewed in House et al., 2014a; Price and D'Andrea, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: There is a genetic interaction between H2A.1 and Pol32 (Polδ) in maintaining CAG repeat stability.
source: Our results demonstrate a genetic interaction between H2A.1 and Pol32 (Polδ) in maintaining CAG repeat stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the epistasis data.

claim: The timing and reading of H2A.1-T126 and other chromatin marks may determine how effectively the Polδ complex moves through the donor strand during repair, ensuring that repair is efficient (timely) and that it proceeds with high-fidelity, limiting mutagenic repair outcomes.
source: The timing and reading of H2A.1-T126 and other chromatin marks may determine how effectively the Polδ complex moves through the donor strand during repair, ensuring that repair is efficient (timely) and that it proceeds with high-fidelity, limiting mutagenic repair outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how H2A.1-T126 affects repair fidelity.

claim: Yeast H2A.1 is a closer homolog of mammalian H2AX, whereas H2A.2 is more functionally equivalent to mammalian H2A.
source: Our results suggest that yeast H2A.1 is a closer homolog of mammalian H2AX, whereas H2A.2 is more functionally equivalent to mammalian H2A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data showing differential roles of H2A.1 and H2A.2.

claim: Although the density of nucleosomes can vary at different genomic loci, the abundance of histones throughout the genome means they are readily available at the frontlines of DNA damage.
source: Although the density of nucleosomes can vary at different genomic loci, the abundance of histones throughout the genome means they are readily available at the frontlines of DNA damage.
evidence: This is a general statement about histone abundance and availability.

claim: In yeast, histone H2A.1 and H2A.2 are both present in a healthy cell and are likely interspersed throughout the genome.
source: In yeast, histone H2A.1 and H2A.2 are both present in a healthy cell and are likely interspersed throughout the genome.
